title: Metallic Materials
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 7 Pre-Technical Studies; not yet checked by a Pre-Technical Studies teacher; safety lines marked SAFETY in the library to confirm first; not loaded by the live tutor

skills.key_step: The learner identifies types of metallic materials in the environment: ferrous (contain iron: cast iron, mild steel) and non-ferrous (copper, aluminium, zinc, lead, tin), and alloys (brass, bronze), using colour, weight, rust and a magnet.

floor.question: Why does a metal spoon get hot in tea?

representations: a metals display: nail, wire, can, key

board.do: Put a nail, copper wire and an aluminium can on the table.

board.say: Will a magnet pick it up? Is it ferrous?

board.do: Wait for the learner to say no, non-ferrous.
Test all three with the magnet.

misconceptions.ask: A silvery, light metal does not stick to a magnet. What is it likely to be?
misconceptions.repair: Test a steel nail and an aluminium can with a magnet and by weight in the hand.
Strip a piece of electric cable and show the reddish-brown copper inside.

misconceptions.ask: A magnet does not pick up a metal spoon. What can you say?
misconceptions.repair: Test a nail, a copper wire, an aluminium can and a brass key with a magnet; only the nail sticks.

listen_for: Aluminium, because it is a strong metal
misconceptions.repair: Teach ferrous = contains iron (iron, steel); non-ferrous = no iron (copper, aluminium, zinc, lead, tin). Test with a magnet and rust.

skills.key_step: The learner describes the physical properties of metals: lustre (shine when cut or polished), conduct heat and electricity, malleable (hammered into sheets), ductile (drawn into wire), strong and hard, some magnetic (iron, steel), iron and steel rust.
representations: a property table with test results
a rusty and a clean nail
steps: Link the property to a use.
contexts: a jiko made of sheet metal

board.do: Write the properties: shine, conduct, malleable, ductile, magnetic, rust.

board.say: Which object in the room shows this property?

board.do: Wait for the learner to name a wire.
Match an object to every property.

misconceptions.ask: Which metal does a magnet pick up?
misconceptions.repair: Test five metals with a magnet and record which stick.
Show a rusty nail, green old copper and a dull aluminium pot; only iron and steel rust (red-brown).

misconceptions.ask: Why does a metal spoon get hot in hot tea?
misconceptions.repair: Put a metal and a plastic spoon in hot water and feel the handles after a minute (with care).

misconceptions.ask: What happens when copper is hammered?
misconceptions.repair: Hammer a short copper wire flat and bend it; compare with a piece of tile (shown, not done by learners).

checks.question: What does malleable mean?
checks.answer: Can be hammered into a sheet

skills.key_step: The learner relates metals to their uses by their properties: copper for electric wires (conducts, ductile), aluminium for sufurias and windows (light, conducts heat, does not rust), steel for tools, nails and frames (hard, strong), galvanised iron for roofing (zinc stops rust).

floor.question: Which property lets copper be drawn into wire?

representations: a use and property matching chart
samples: cable, sufuria, nail, roofing offcut
a "what must it do?" question card
steps: Ask what the metal must do.

board.do: Write three uses: electric wire, sufuria, jembe blade.

board.say: Which metal, and which property makes it right?

board.do: Wait for the learner to say aluminium, light and conducts heat.

misconceptions.repair: Strip a cable and show copper; say copper conducts electricity very well and bends easily.

misconceptions.ask: Why is a sufuria often made of aluminium?
misconceptions.repair: Weigh an aluminium sufuria and a steel one of the same size; aluminium is light and conducts heat.

listen_for: Because it does not conduct heat
misconceptions.ask: Why is steel used for a jembe blade?
misconceptions.repair: For each use, ask "what must the metal do here?" then pick the property.

misconceptions.ask: Why are iron roofing sheets galvanised (coated with zinc)?
misconceptions.repair: Show a new and an old roofing sheet; rust starts where the zinc coat is scratched. Name galvanising.

checks.question: Which metal is used for electric wire?
Why is a jembe blade made of steel?
